\begin{align*}y''-2y'+2y&=2e^x\cos x-2e^x(\sin x+\cos x)+2e^x\sin x\\&=2e^x\cos x-2e^x\sin x-2e^x\cos x+2e^x\sin x\\&=0\end{align*}

content.prompt: If $y=e^{-x}\cos x$, find $y'$ and $y''$, and show that $y''+2y'+2y=0$.

answer.worked:
$$\begin{align*}y'&=-e^{-x}\cos x+e^{-x}(-\sin x)\\&=-e^{-x}(\cos x+\sin x)\\y''&=e^{-x}(\cos x+\sin x)+(-e^{-x})(-\sin x+\cos x)\\&=e^{-x}(\cos x+\sin x)-e^{-x}(\cos x-\sin x)\\&=e^{-x}(2\sin x)\end{align*}$$

$$\begin{align*}y''+2y'+2y&=2e^{-x}\sin x+2(-e^{-x})(\cos x+\sin x)+2e^{-x}\cos x\\&=2e^{-x}\sin x-2e^{-x}\cos x-2e^{-x}\sin x+2e^{-x}\cos x\\&=0\end{align*}$$

content.prompt: If $f(x)=\log_e\left(\dfrac{1+\sin x}{\cos x}\right)$, show that $f'(x)=\sec x$.

answer.worked: $$\begin{align*}f(x)&=\ln|1+\sin x|-\ln|\cos x|\\f'(x)&=\frac{\cos x}{1+\sin x}-\frac{-\sin x}{\cos x}\\&=\frac{\cos x}{1+\sin x}+\frac{\sin x}{\cos x}\\&=\frac{\cos^2x+\sin x(1+\sin x)}{\cos x(1+\sin x)}\\&=\frac{\cos^2x+\sin x+\sin^2x}{\cos x(1+\sin x)}\\&=\frac{1+\sin x}{\cos x(1+\sin x)}\\&=\frac{1}{\cos x}\\&=\sec x\end{align*}$$

content.prompt: If $y=\ln\left(\frac{\sqrt2-\cos x}{\sqrt2+\cos x}\right)$, show that $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=\dfrac{2\sqrt2\sin x}{1+\sin^2x}$.

answer.worked: $$\begin{align*}y&=\ln(\sqrt2-\cos x)-\ln(\sqrt2+\cos x)\\\frac{dy}{dx}&=\frac{\sin x}{\sqrt2-\cos x}-\frac{-\sin x}{\sqrt2+\cos x}\\\frac{dy}{dx}&=\frac{\sin x}{\sqrt2-\cos x}+\frac{\sin x}{\sqrt2+\cos x}\\\frac{dy}{dx}&=\frac{\sin x(\sqrt2+\cos x)+\sin x(\sqrt2-\cos x)}{(\sqrt2-\cos x)(\sqrt2+\cos x)}\\\frac{dy}{dx}&=\frac{\sin x(2\sqrt2)}{2-\cos^2x}\\\frac{dy}{dx}&=\frac{2\sqrt2\sin x}{2-\cos^2x}\\\frac{dy}{dx}&=\frac{2\sqrt2\sin x}{1+1-\cos^2x}\\\frac{dy}{dx}&=\frac{2\sqrt2\sin x}{1+\sin^2x}.\end{align*}$$

answer.worked:
The tangent $x-y=\frac{\pi}{4}-\frac12$ meets the $x$-axis where $y=0$:
$$\begin{align*}x&=\frac{\pi}{4}-\frac12,\\P&=\left(\frac{\pi}{4}-\frac12,0\right).\end{align*}$$
The normal $x+y=\frac{\pi}{4}+\frac12$ meets the $y$-axis where $x=0$:
$$\begin{align*}y&=\frac{\pi}{4}+\frac12,\\Q&=\left(0,\frac{\pi}{4}+\frac12\right).\end{align*}$$
Since the coordinate axes are perpendicular,
$$\begin{align*}\operatorname{Area}(\triangle OPQ)&=\frac12|OP||OQ|\\&=\frac12\left(\frac{\pi}{4}-\frac12\right)\left(\frac{\pi}{4}+\frac12\right)\\&=\frac12\left[\left(\frac{\pi}{4}\right)^2-\left(\frac12\right)^2\right]\\&=\frac12\left(\frac{\pi^2}{16}-\frac14\right)\\&=\frac1{32}(\pi^2-4)\\&=\frac{\pi^2-4}{32}\text{ units}^2.\end{align*}$$

The tangent has gradient $m=-\pi$ and passes through $P(\pi,0)$:
$$\begin{align*}y-y_1&=m(x-x_1)\\y-0&=-\pi(x-\pi)\\y&=-\pi x+\pi^2\end{align*}$$

content.prompt:
The graphs of $y=e\ln x$ and $y=ax^2+c$ are shown.

The line $y=x$ is a tangent to both graphs at their point of intersection.

Find the values of $a$ and $c$.

spec.description: Unscaled black coordinate sketch with positive axis arrows, no ticks or grid, upward parabola with vertex above the origin, increasing concave-down logarithmic curve and line through the origin. All three meet with common tangency in the first quadrant; each graph has arrowed extensions. The source origin label is omitted under the graph convention.
spec.mathematics: For construction only, coordinates are normalised by e on both axes: the curves are Y=(X²+1)/2, Y=1+ln X and Y=X, tangent at (1,1). No numerical values or parameter answers are printed.
spec.answerVisibility: All source-given curve identities and tangency relationships are visible; derived parameter values remain hidden.

answer.worked:
$$\begin{aligned}y&=e\ln x\quad(1)&y&=ax^2+c\quad(2)\\y'&=\frac ex&y'&=2ax\end{aligned}$$
At the point of tangency, the gradient is $1$.
$$\begin{align*}\frac ex&=1\\x&=e\end{align*}$$
At $x=e$, the derivative of (2) is also $1$:
$$\begin{align*}2ae&=1\\a&=\frac{1}{2e}\end{align*}$$
Using (1),
$$\begin{align*}y&=e\ln e\\y&=e\end{align*}$$
The point of tangency is $(e,e)$. Since this point lies on (2),
$$\begin{align*}e&=\left(\frac{1}{2e}\right)e^2+c\\c&=\frac e2\end{align*}$$
Therefore $a=\dfrac{1}{2e}$ and $c=\dfrac e2$.

answer.worked:
$$\begin{align*}y&=c\ln x\\\frac{dy}{dx}&=\frac{c}{x}\end{align*}$$
At $x=p$, the gradient is $m=\dfrac{c}{p}$ and the tangent passes through $(p,c\ln p)$.
Therefore the tangent has equation
$$\begin{align*}y-c\ln p&=\frac{c}{p}(x-p)\\y&=\frac{cx}{p}-c+c\ln p.\end{align*}$$

children.label: b

answer.worked:
For a gradient of $1$,
$$\begin{align*}\frac{c}{p}&=1\\c&=p.\end{align*}$$
Since the tangent passes through $(0,0)$, substitute $p=c$ into the equation from part a:
$$\begin{align*}0&=-c+c\ln c\\0&=c(\ln c-1)\\\ln c&=1\qquad(c>0)\\c&=e.\end{align*}$$

spec.sourceRegion: Supplied answer sketch below the parts, left side

spec.mathematics: The curve is y=e^{2x}; its tangent through the origin is y=2ex, touching at (1/2,e).

answer.worked:
$$\begin{aligned}y&=e^{2x}\\\frac{dy}{dx}&=2e^{2x}\end{aligned}$$
The gradient of $y=mx$ is $m$. At $P$, the gradients are equal.
$$\begin{aligned}2e^{2x}&=m\\e^{2x}&=\frac m2\\\ln(e^{2x})&=\ln\left(\frac m2\right)\\2x&=\ln\left(\frac m2\right)\\x&=\frac12\ln\left(\frac m2\right)\end{aligned}$$
Substitute into the curve:
$$\begin{aligned}y&=e^{2\times\frac12\ln(m/2)}\\y&=e^{\ln(m/2)}\\y&=\frac m2\end{aligned}$$
Thus $P\left(\frac12\ln\left(\frac m2\right),\frac m2\right)$. Using $m=2e$ from part c gives $P\left(\frac12,e\right)$.

The line $y=mx$ passes through $(0,0)$ and $P\left(\frac12\ln\left(\frac m2\right),\frac m2\right)$. Using the gradient formula,
$$\begin{aligned}\frac{\frac m2-0}{\frac12\ln(m/2)-0}&=m\\\frac{\frac m2}{\frac12\ln(m/2)}&=m\\\frac{m}{\ln(m/2)}&=m\end{aligned}$$
Since $m=2e^{2x}>0$,
$$\begin{aligned}\ln\left(\frac m2\right)&=1\\\frac m2&=e^1\\m&=2e\end{aligned}$$

teachingContext.methodNote: The supplied solution on page 17 equates the derivative to m, solves with logarithms for the coordinates in terms of m, then applies the gradient formula between the origin and P to obtain m=2e. No separate teaching pages were supplied.

entries.description: If y = e^x sin x, find y′ and y″, and show that y″ − 2y′ + 2y = 0.
entries.presentation: Question in black; supplied working in blue beneath it. Preserve space for differentiation and substitution.

entries.expectedAnswer:
y′ = e^x sin x + e^x cos x
   = e^x(sin x + cos x)
y″ = e^x(sin x + cos x) + e^x(cos x − sin x)
   = e^x(2 cos x)

y″ − 2y′ + 2y = 2e^x cos x − 2e^x(sin x + cos x) + 2e^x sin x
               = 2e^x cos x − 2e^x sin x − 2e^x cos x + 2e^x sin x
               = 0
entries.presentation: Two working groups: derivatives, then verification. Keep continuation relations aligned.

entries.description: If y = e^(−x) cos x, find y′ and y″, and show that y″ + 2y′ + 2y = 0.
entries.presentation: Question in black; supplied working in blue beneath it. Preserve space for differentiation and substitution.

entries.expectedAnswer:
y′ = −e^(−x) cos x + e^(−x)(−sin x) = −e^(−x)(cos x + sin x)
y″ = e^(−x)(cos x + sin x) + (−e^(−x))(−sin x + cos x)
   = e^(−x)(cos x + sin x) − e^(−x)(cos x − sin x)
   = e^(−x)(2 sin x)

y″ + 2y′ + 2y = 2e^(−x) sin x + 2(−e^(−x))(cos x + sin x) + 2e^(−x) cos x
               = 2e^(−x) sin x − 2e^(−x) cos x − 2e^(−x) sin x + 2e^(−x) cos x
               = 0

entries.description: If f(x) = log_e((1 + sin x)/cos x), show that f′(x) = sec x.

entries.expectedAnswer:
f(x) = ln(1 + sin x) − ln(cos x)
f′(x) = cos x/(1 + sin x) − (−sin x)/cos x
      = cos x/(1 + sin x) + sin x/cos x
      = [cos²x + sin x(1 + sin x)]/[cos x(1 + sin x)]
      = [cos²x + sin x + sin²x]/[cos x(1 + sin x)]
      = (1 + sin x)/[cos x(1 + sin x)]
      = 1/cos x
      = sec x
